qt.t:
Per @Liz_Friden The U.S. is sending the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit to the Middle East, two U.S. officials confirm to Fox News. The ships will arrive in the Middle East by the end of November, the officials said. These new deployments will add about 10,000 Sailors and Marines to the Middle East.

The USS Roosevelt will be the third aircraft carrier in the Middle East, joining the USS George H.W. Bush which arrived to the region in April, and the USS George Washington which arrived in mid-August to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln. This will provide more options for the U.S. as President Trump is reportedly considering ramping up strikes on Iran after the Midterms. 

The USS Roosevelt departed its home port of San Diego on Sunday and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit deployed from San Diego on Monday along with the Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group. The Marine Expeditionary Unit and Amphibious Ready Group typically include about 4,200 Marines and Sailors. The USS Roosevelt carrier strike group includes about 6,000 Sailors.

cvn-71.tx:
The USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN-71) carrier strike group and the USS Makin Island (LHD-8) amphibious ready group, with the embarked 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit (MEU), are headed to the Middle East, two U.S. officials told Fox News. The ships are expected to arrive by the end of November, adding about 10,000 sailors and Marines to the region. Fox reports about 6,000 are in the carrier strike group and about 4,200 in the MEU and Makin Island group, a typical size for such a force.

The Roosevelt would be the third aircraft carrier in the Middle East, joining the USS George H.W. Bush (CVN-77) and USS George Washington (CVN-73). Makin Island would be the second amphibious assault ship with an embarked MEU in the region, alongside USS Boxer (LHD-4) and the 11th MEU. The deployment comes as President Trump has said renewed military action against Iran remains possible after the November 3 midterm elections.

lhd-4.t: If you want to understand what it means to be an American citizen, look at what happened in the Indian Ocean on Easter Sunday, April 12, 2009. One merchant cap…
lhd-4.tx:
If you want to understand what it means to be an American citizen, look at what happened in the Indian Ocean on Easter Sunday, April 12, 2009.

One merchant captain from Vermont named Richard Phillips was being held hostage inside a covered orange lifeboat by Somali pirates armed with AK-47s.

He was not a general. He was not a politician. He was one cargo ship captain who had offered himself as a hostage to save his crew.

To bring that one man home, the United States sent the guided-missile destroyer USS Bainbridge, the frigate USS Halyburton, the amphibious assault ship USS Boxer, and a team of U.S. Navy SEALs who parachuted straight into the black ocean at night.

For four days, the lifeboat pitched violently in rough seas twenty-five yards behind the destroyer.

Then at dusk on Sunday, a pirate pressed the barrel of his AK-47 directly against Captain Phillips' back and prepared to kill him.

On the fantail of the USS Bainbridge, three Navy SEAL snipers lay braced in the dark. The destroyer was rolling in one direction. The tiny lifeboat was pitching in another. If even one sniper missed by half an inch, or fired a tenth of a second late, the hostage would die.

Through night-vision scopes, all three snipers waited for the exact millisecond when three targets appeared in the tiny windows at once.

One word came over the headset.

cvn-76.t: If anyone ever tells you the United States military is only a machine of war, take them to the coast of Tohoku, Japan, and tell them what happened in March 201…
cvn-76.tx:
If anyone ever tells you the United States military is only a machine of war, take them to the coast of Tohoku, Japan, and tell them what happened in March 2011.

When the 9.0 earthquake and 40-foot tsunami wiped out entire towns and crippled the Fukushima nuclear plant, foreign embassies told their citizens to flee Japan immediately.

The USS Ronald Reagan Carrier Strike Group did the exact opposite.
They steamed at flank speed straight TOWARD the disaster zone.

When the first Navy helicopters touched down in the snow along the northern coast, nineteen-year-old American sailors saw something they will never forget:

Thousands of Japanese mothers, grandmothers, and small children huddled in freezing dark shelters. Their shoes had been ripped off by the black water. Their coats were soaked in icy mud.

Official relief cargo planes were still days away.
The sailors of the USS Ronald Reagan, USS Chancellorsville, and USS Preble didn't wait for orders from Washington.

They walked back to their own narrow bunks below deck and opened their personal lockers.

In just a few hours, young American sailors stripped off their own warm clothes to send ashore on the next helicopter.
The official Navy log still records what they gave from their own sea bags that afternoon:

• 748 pairs of their own socks
• 311 jackets and sweaters
• 450 shirts and 237 pairs of pants
• 57 pairs of their own shoes
• Over 100 blankets right off their racks

And here is the detail that makes grown men in Japan weep to this day:

Included in those boxes were 20 stuffed animals.
Tough nineteen-year-old sailors took the lucky teddy bears and plush toys their moms and little sisters had tucked into their sea bags back home in America—and sent them to crying Japanese children so they wouldn't be scared in the dark.

Days later, as Navy helicopters flew low over the ruined coast, pilots looked down through tears at a muddy schoolyard.
Japanese children had gathered broken white debris to spell one giant word on the ground for the American sky:

“ARIGATO.” (Thank you.)

Fifty thousand Americans came to save us in Operation Tomodachi.
In Japanese, “Tomodachi” means friend.
In our hearts, it means brother. Forever. 🇺🇸🤝🇯🇵

🇺🇸 U.S. Navy has doubled its fleet capacity to operate the MQ-25A Stingray unmanned aircraft system (UAS) over a five-month period, standing up a second operational MD-5C Ground Control Station (GCS). @USNavy 

MD-5C, powered by Lockheed Martin Skunk Works MDCX autonomy platform, is installed in the Unmanned Air Warfare Center (UAWC), the dedicated shipboard command center for unmanned carrier aviation. The Navy's Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN 71) received the first operational MD-5C in March 2026, followed by her sister ship USS Ronald Reagan (CVN 76) in August 2026. @LockheedMartin 

The MD-5C is a highly complex system-of-systems, which includes the government Command, Control, Communications, Computers and Intelligence (C4I) network, MDCX software and hardware, and additional government-produced ancillary equipment. Within the GCS, MDCX is the mission planning and execution software that enables Navy operators to command and control the MQ-25A Stingray, extending carrier air wing reach and freeing manned aircraft for higher-priority missions.

This marked the first time the aircraft was controlled from a carrier using the ground control station and Navy communications network used in operational missions.

The test validated an end-to-end BLOS C2 capability over the Navy’s operational command, control, communications, computers, and intelligence (C4I) network enabling shipboard teams can reliably monitor and command the MQ-25A from an aircraft carrier.

This demonstration is one in a series of buildup exercises designed to validate procedures, networks and interfaces ahead of a risk reduction flight-test program that will include carrier at-sea operations.

The carrier in the Pacific linked to the aircraft at Boeing’s facility in Mascoutah, Illinois, via an MD-5C ground station and a low-Earth-orbit satellite network. It is a beyond-line-of-sight command test, not a refuelling flight. The Reagan’s Unmanned Air Warfare Center was installed after 11 ship modifications. The Theodore Roosevelt got the first operational MD-5C in March.

The Stingray is 15.54 metres (51 feet) long with a 22.86-metre (75-foot) span. It is meant to offload 6,350 kilograms (14,000 pounds) of fuel at 926 kilometres (500 nautical miles). The programme covers 76 aircraft, including 67 operational tankers, at about $19.4 billion, with initial operational capability planned for 2029. 

It is intended to free Super Hornets from tanker duty.

suez.tx:
70 years ago today, on the 22nd of October 1956, France, Britain and Israel started negotiating a sinister deal at Sèvres. Israel would attack Egypt. France and Britain would order both sides to retreat. Nasser would refuse. France and Britain would then a have a casus belli to bomb Egypt. 

On 30 October 1956, Britain and France issued an ultimatum to Egypt and Israel. Stop fighting, withdraw your armies from the Suez Canal, or we will intervene to restore peace.

Sounds ever so benign, right? 

Or ever so cunning. 

They had secretly arranged the war themselves.

A few months earlier, Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser had nationalised the Suez Canal Company, which had been controlled by British and French interests.

The canal was on Egyptian territory, but Britain and France were used to deciding what happened there.

Nasser wanted the canal's revenues to help finance the Aswan High Dam, after the USA and Britain withdrew their offers to help finance its construction.

London was furious. 

Paris was 'pas amusé' either to say the least. French elites had special beef with Nasser over his support for the Algerian struggle against French colonial rule.

Israel had its own reasons to confront Egypt, including Egyptian restrictions on Israeli shipping and violent cross-border conflict.

Three governments with different grievances came together in one of history's most cynical ways. 

On 22 October 1956, senior representatives of Britain, France and Israel gathered secretly at Sèvres, outside Paris.

Among the Israeli participants were Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion, Moshe Dayan and Shimon Peres.

Over the following days they worked out a devious plan.

Israel would invade Egypt's Sinai Peninsula.

Britain and France would then demand that both sides withdraw from the Suez Canal.

Egypt would have to withdraw its forces from part of its own territory and allow foreign troops to occupy strategic positions along the canal.

The planners expected Nasser to refuse.

That refusal would give Britain and France their excuse to attack Egypt.

The agreement was signed on 24 October.

Five days later, Israel invaded.

On 30 October, Britain and France delivered their ultimatum.

The following day, British and French aircraft began bombing Egyptian targets.

Port Said got treated to bombardment, fighting and civilian casualties.

But then the plan ran into obstacles.

American president Dwight Eisenhower refused to support the operation. 

Washington applied enormous diplomatic and financial pressure. 

The Soviet Union threatened intervention.

Britain and France accepted a ceasefire on 6 November.

The invasion became a political humiliation. Nasser remained in power, and Egypt retained control of the canal.

It wasn't bad enough. Officials had to add shameless hypocrisy to the mix. 

On 20 December 1956, British Prime Minister Anthony Eden told the House of Commons that his government had possessed no foreknowledge that Israel would attack Egypt.

Yet British representatives had participated in the negotiations specifying precisely when Israel would attack.

The British diplomat who signed the secret agreement, Patrick Dean, had even returned to Paris the following day in an effort to destroy copies of the document.

Mortifying. 

Israel had to add sickening cruelty to the stinking cocktail. 

On 3 November 1956, during Israel's invasion of Egypt, Israeli troops occupied Khan Yunis in Gaza. There 275 Palestinians were reported killed, according to the UN. 

Palestinian witnesses described the killing of unarmed civilians, while Israel claimed its soldiers had encountered armed resistance.

Abdel Aziz al-Rantisi, 9 at the time, could hear the whole town wailing and wailing. Joe Sacco and Chris Hedges spoke to him decades ago and recently mentioned this haunting detail at a talk about their new book, Requiem for Gaza. 

That's how it goes. Elites hatch neat plans in warm rooms with delicious food, apathetic to who will be squished.

On this day—October 23, 1942

An SS Einsatzkommando unit was waiting in Athens for the order to bring the Holocaust to Mandate Palestine’s Jews when British forces under Montgomery opened the Second Battle of El Alamein.

By the summer of 1942, Erwin Rommel’s Afrika Korps had driven deep into Egypt. British forces held a defensive line at El Alamein, 60 miles west of Alexandria. From there, the road to the Suez Canal and to Mandate Palestine with nearly 600,000 Jews was open. Another 75,000 lived in Egypt, and both communities understood the danger. Reports of mass killings of Jews in Europe had already reached them.

In Berlin, an Einsatzkommando under Walther Rauff was assembled and positioned in Athens. Its orders were to carry out “special operations” against the Jewish population once Axis forces advanced beyond Egypt. Local Arabs in Mandate Palestine, anticipating a German arrival, marked Jewish houses for seizure. Grandi Mufti Amin al-Husseini had already met with Hitler and sought Arab units to fight alongside German forces against the Jews and the British.

On the night of October 23, Montgomery’s Eighth Army launched a massive artillery barrage and infantry assault. Over the following days, the Axis lines broke. Rommel’s forces began a long retreat to the west. The Einsatzkommando never deployed to Mandate Palestine, but it later operated in Tunisia.

The battle is usually remembered as a turning point in the North African campaign. For the Jews of Mandate Palestine and Egypt, it was the point at which a planned extension of the Holocaust was halted.

Why Egypt will eventually be pulled into the war in Yemen on Saudi Arabia's side directly. 

I was one of the first accounts over 5 months back that told my readers Egypt would enter the Middle East war. 

I do not look at what governments say alone, I look at data, its needs, wants and necessities. I saw that the war in the Middle East was becoming an Existential War for Egypt even though Egypt is on a different continent and in the outer periphery of the war between Iran and USA …

The reason I saw was economic pressure and financial.

Egypt carries a chronic, structural weakness that has shadowed it for decades, and that weakness is its currency. 

The Egyptian pound keeps devaluing, inflation keeps climbing, and the state stays upright only by getting its hands on hard currency, US dollars, to keep itself standing.

The numbers make it concrete. Egypt is roughly a $380 to $400 billion dollar economy, but what holds it together is the foreign currency it pulls in from outside, and that comes from three pillars. 

All three run straight through the stability of this region.

The first is the Suez Canal. Ships pay their tolls in hard currency, and at its peak the canal earned Egypt about $9.4 billion dollars a year. 

Since the Ansarallah Houthis started hitting the Red Sea, traffic has rerouted around Africa and that revenue has fallen by roughly half, with Sisi himself saying the canal has lost close to $9 billion dollars over two years. This is already happening, not a future risk.

The second is tourism, worth a record $15 to $17 billion dollars a year, and nothing empties the Red Sea resorts and the hotels faster than a regional war that’s on international media coverage everyday for months…

The third is the blind spot almost no one counts, human capital. 

Millions of Egyptians work across the Gulf, the largest numbers in Saudi Arabia, around a million in the UAE, and more spread through Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, Iraq and Jordan. 

What they send home is Egypt's single biggest source of foreign currency, a record of over $37 billion dollars last year. 

When a region goes to war and economies seize up, foreigners and expats are the first workers let go, so those Egyptians get sent home, their dollars stop arriving, and the lifeline thins out at the EXACT moment Egypt needs it most.

Those three pillars, worth more than $55 billion dollars a YEAR together, are the dollar engine of the entire country, and every one of them is directly exposed to this war.

All of it can break at once. The Red Sea stays closed, Suez income falls, tourism dries up and Gulf remittances shrink together, which drains the dollars holding up the pound, pushes the currency down further, drives inflation harder, and corners a country of over 100 million people into the kind of economic pain that governments do not want and can endanger its survival…

At that point Egypt is no longer choosing. Its dollar lifelines all depend on reopening the Red Sea and calming the Gulf, and the force choking that artery is the Houthis in Yemen. 

Protecting the canal, the tourists and the workers stops being “economic policy” and becomes a “national security necessity”, which is how a state ends up at war whether it wanted to or not. L

And, this is why Egypt cannot stay on the sidelines anymore. 

It joins because the war has reached its wallet, not out of any appetite for the fight, and that is the difference between a “Coalition of the Willing” and the “Coalition of the Forced” this has become, one more state pulled in as the conflict widens and swallows the region.

The war continues…

suez.t: October 23, 1942. At twenty minutes to ten at night, in the desert of Egypt, more than eight hundred British guns open fire at once, and the darkness erupts in…
suez.tx:
October 23, 1942. At twenty minutes to ten at night, in the desert of Egypt, more than eight hundred British guns open fire at once, and the darkness erupts into a wall of flame and thunder that can be felt in the chest from miles away. The Second Battle of El Alamein has begun. It is the battle that will finally break Rommel in the desert, the hinge of the whole war in North Africa, and the victory that Churchill would say marked "the end of the beginning."

I have been following the desert war since the early days of this series, Rommel the Desert Fox running the British ragged back and forth across Libya and Egypt, the see-saw campaign that had swung all the way to El Alamein, the last defensible line before the Nile, the Suez Canal, and the oil of the Middle East. In the summer Rommel had been stopped there, barely, in the first battle. Now the British Eighth Army had a new commander, Bernard Montgomery, a careful, methodical, supremely confident general who had rebuilt the army's morale and refused to attack until he had overwhelming strength.

And by October he had it. Montgomery had built up a crushing superiority, in men, in tanks, in guns, in aircraft, in supplies, far more than Rommel could match, because the Axis supply line across the Mediterranean was being strangled while the British were pouring reinforcements, including masses of new American-built Sherman tanks, into Egypt. Rommel himself was away sick in Germany when the blow fell, his army dug in behind vast belts of mines and wire the Germans grimly called the "Devil's Gardens."

Montgomery's plan was not clever maneuver but deliberate, grinding attrition, a battle he called "crumbling." It opened on the night of the 23rd with one of the greatest artillery bombardments since the First World War, those eight hundred-plus guns firing in a stupendous barrage that announced the offensive and smashed at the Axis positions. Then the infantry went in, in the moonlight, to clear paths through the enormous minefields so the armor could pass, and the fighting settled into a brutal, close-quarters slog through the mines and the dug-in defenses.

It was not quick. For days the battle hung in the balance, the British grinding forward yard by yard through the Devil's Gardens, taking heavy losses, the attack at times seeming to stall. Rommel rushed back from Germany to take command, but he had no answer to Montgomery's material superiority and his relentless pressure, and critically he was running out of fuel, his tanks increasingly immobilized for lack of petrol. Montgomery kept up the attrition, wearing the Axis forces down, destroying tanks he could replace and Rommel could not, until at last, in early November, he concentrated his armor and punched through.

Rommel's front broke. Against Hitler's furious orders to stand and die, Rommel, to save what was left of his army, began a long retreat westward across the desert, a withdrawal that would not stop for hundreds of miles. The Axis army in the desert had been decisively beaten for the first time, and it would never recover the initiative. Combined with the Anglo-American landings in northwest Africa that came just days later, El Alamein doomed the entire Axis position in North Africa.

The victory meant an enormous amount, and not just militarily. It was the first great, clear-cut British land victory over the Germans in the whole war, coming after years of defeats and retreats, and it was desperately needed for Allied morale. Church bells were rung in Britain to celebrate. Churchill captured its meaning in one of his famous lines: "Now this is not the end. It is not even the beginning of the end. But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning." The tide in the west had turned, and it turned here, in the desert, beginning with those eight hundred guns firing into the dark on the night of the 23rd.

Gideon Rachman asks whether the world is “sleepwalking into World War III?”

It’s a long read, and not a terribly enlightening one. Rachman tours Ukraine, the Gulf, the Taiwan Strait and the 65 conflicts currently raging around the world, and finds the culprits to be “revisionist powers”, “strongman leaders” and an “axis of adversaries”: Russia, China, Iran and North Korea.

In a couple of thousand words, he finds no space at all for the crisis of neoliberal capitalism, albeit he does note the important fact that the G7, which accounted for two-thirds of world output in 1989, is now down to 43 percent.

Lenin would have recognised the connection between this decline and the attempt by declining powers to use military means to hold on to a world they can no longer dominate economically. He would have easily recognised “the striving for domination, not for freedom”.

More than a century after his death, Lenin remains a far better and more relevant guide to the questions of war and peace than the FT’s chief foreign affairs commentator.

Imperialism is hitting out in all directions:

• Genocide in Gaza, armed and financed by Washington, London and Berlin.

• US-Israeli criminal war on Iran and Lebanon.

• A proxy war in Ukraine to weaken and dismember Russia.

• Economic warfare against China: tariffs, chip bans, sanctions, blacklists.

• A “Donroe Doctrine” under which a president is kidnapped, Cuba is placed under a genocidal energy siege, and election results are determined in Washington DC.

• AUKUS, RIMPAC, Talisman Sabre, and a ring of US bases around China’s coast.

None of this features as a cause of insecurity in Rachman’s telling. He’s more worried about whether Xi Jinping “considers that America’s Taiwan Relations Act means something”, or whether Putin sees NATO’s Article Five as an “iconclad commitment”.

In other words, his proposed path to peace is for the US to make its threats more credible. Peace through NATO. Peace through imperialism.

The real guarantee of peace is a multipolar world where no power gets to dictate terms to the rest – exactly what Rachman’s “axis of adversaries” is working towards, and exactly what the West is fighting to prevent.

Similar to the House of Saud gaining U.S. support by recycling oil profits into U.S. treasuries, and Bahrain through hosting U.S. naval forces after taking over when the British withdrew east of Suez, Qatar built the largest air base in the Middle East, Al Udeid following the first Gulf War at over $1 billion and invited the U.S. 

Qatar security became synonymous with U.S. national security interest. Now the Qataris are shifting strategies by buying U.S. LNG after Ras Laffan took missile hits. 

The contract to buy U.S. LNG is for about 5% of Qatar capacity, and they already own 70% of Golden Pass LNG in Texas, so they are diversifying their long term supply outside chokepoints. 

Would Qatar bother if they thought the world was going back to the way things were? 

They are buying long term LNG contracts that don't start until the next U.S. administration and run through 2054. 

Is Qatar being clear eyed about a shift in U.S. policy and aligning themselves with the U.S.'s new policy of selling energy instead of guaranteeing security?

ras-laffan.tx:
Since the outbreak of the Iran war in February, Tehran has focused primarily on imposing costs on the US and its Arab regional partners, particularly by targeting military bases and critical infrastructure across the Persian Gulf.

Israel has also been targeted, but generally less heavily than during the June 2025 war.

The clearest example came in March, when Israel struck Iran's South Pars gas facilities. Rather than retaliating primarily against Israel, Iran struck Qatar's Ras Laffan gas complex, inflicting major damage.

Tehran's central deterrence equation was with Washington: make attacks on Iranian energy infrastructure costly enough for the US and its regional partners (and the global economy by extension) that Trump would restrain Israel. And indeed, Trump subsequently declared on Truth Social that Israel would not strike South Pars again.

Iran also hit Israel's Bazan refinery in March, but the damage was less severe than in June 2025, when Iranian strikes shut down the facility and disrupted operations for months.

Now, amid signs that major fighting could soon resume, Tehran appears to be signaling a renewed focus on establishing deterrence directly against Israel, warning of far greater costs should it attack Iran again.

The IRGC spokesperson has threatened that attacks on Iranian energy infrastructure would leave Israel facing "scorched earth."

Separately, IRGC-affiliated Saberin News had circulated a claim that Iran has decided to use “hypersonic penetrator warheads” against Israeli nuclear facilities if its own are attacked. This purported decision remains unverified.

Yet the emerging message appears to be that Israel itself, not just US partners across the Persian Gulf, could face heavier costs in another round. Still, Iranian strategic deception cannot be ruled out, with Tehran potentially seeking to draw US attention and air defenses toward one theater while striking elsewhere.

Furthermore, successfully penetrating Israeli defenses and inflicting damage on that scale would be more difficult for Iran than in the Persian Gulf. But Iran demonstrated in June 2025 and in 2024 that it could do so (as well as recent precision strikes in Jordan). 

In any case, for Trump and Netanyahu, another escalation would be another huge gamble, even moreso if Tehran is now prepared to impose greater costs directly on Israel rather than relying primarily on pressure through the Persian Gulf.

🚨Qatar, sitting on the world's largest gas field, just signed up to buy big volumes of American #LNG through 2054. Let that sink in.

To paraphrase Ronald Reagan's 1984 campaign ad, It's Morning in America's LNG Industry.

Key points:

• Cheniere signed deals to supply @QatarEnergyLNG with up to 4 million tonnes a year from #SabinePass in Louisiana and Corpus Christi in Texas. Deliveries start in 2031.

• Reuters reports Qatar is also in advanced talks with @Venture_Global for at least 3 million more tonnes a year.

• Why? With #Hormuz largely blocked and Ras Laffan damaged, the world's #2 LNG exporter is buying a hedge on the U.S. Gulf Coast.

• The price gap is enormous. Asian spot LNG hit $29.30/MMBtu last week, while Henry Hub sits around $2.84. That's roughly 10 to 1.

• U.S. LNG feedgas demand topped a record 20 Bcf/d on Oct. 19 as Golden Pass ramps up.

• And the fear that exports would drive up U.S. prices? It was never anything more than a leftwing talking point. Not happening. Storage is 35 Bcf above the five-year average, and Henry Hub is under $3.

The lesson here is simple: when even your competitors sign 20-plus-year contracts for your product, the debate is over. 

American #naturalgas isn't a short-lived "bridge fuel." It's the backbone of global energy security, and the world's buyers are voting with their checkbooks.

IRAN THREATENS TO TURN OFF THE INTERNET. THE INTERNET CHECKS ITS NOTES. 🛜

The IRGC's spokesman, Hossein Mohebi, says seven cables run under the Strait of Hormuz and "the world's internet and commercial data depend on" them. Then, to show he's serious, he posted a picture of a missile on X that appears to be AI-generated.

Sir. You threatened the internet. On the internet. With AI art.

Let's look at these world-ending cables.

📡 The International Cable Protection Committee counts FIVE active cable segments crossing the strait. Not seven. Even his threat got inflated.

📡 Those cables carry less than 1% of the world's international bandwidth. One percent. Netflix buffering in Bahrain is not the collapse of Western civilization.

📡 There are hundreds of undersea cables on the planet, and they average about 199 faults a year. Four a week, and about two thirds of that is fishing boats and ship anchors. Somewhere a guy named Sven dragged a trawl net across a cable this morning, and nobody gave him a press conference.

📡 In 2024 a ship the Houthis sank dragged its anchor across the Red Sea floor and cut three cables at once. You know what happened? Carriers rerouted the traffic through other cables, the US and China, and the rest of us kept doomscrolling. Routing around damage is the internet's whole point. Americans figured that out in the 1960s.

So who would this hurt? Here's the funny part.

🇦🇪 The UAE lands most of its cables at Fujairah, outside the strait.
🇸🇦 Saudi Arabia mostly uses its Red Sea coast.
🇮🇶 Iraq's only two international cables run through Iranian waters.

So the IRGC's master plan to cut off the "enemy" would mostly knock their buddies in Baghdad offline. Galaxy brain stuff.

And let's be real about who the champion of cutting off Iran's internet is. Iran. Tehran has pulled the plug on its own people again and again whenever they protest. The only country these guys have ever successfully taken offline is their own.

Meanwhile their colleague Mohsen Rezaei says $2 trillion of data centers would be "within our range." Which ones? He didn't say. How'd he get $2 trillion? He didn't say. The math came from the same place as the missile picture.

To be fair, they've tried. Back in March their drones hit Amazon data centers in the UAE and Bahrain. It caused a fire, a power cut and a nasty outage. And then AWS told customers to fail over to another region. That's it. That's the cloud. It's called the cloud because it's not in one building, fellas.

Destroy $2 trillion of data centers? Unless the IRGC has cut a deal with Godzilla, I'm not worried. And even Godzilla would need a few sequels.

Do they overestimate their awesomeness? These are the guys who announced a "Persian Gulf Data Authority" while the US Navy is parked in their front yard. That's a man in a bathrobe declaring himself mayor of the cul de sac.

Gentlemen, a friendly tip from someone who has spent 20 years in IT: before you threaten the global network, maybe learn how it works. And be careful with your own gadgets. Ask Hezbollah how much they enjoyed their pagers. 📟

Have you tried turning your threats off and back on again? 🦋

fujairah.tx:
On the 29th of July, 800 kilometres of the Red Sea went to war. No navy was involved. Nobody fired a shot. 4 men in London moved a line on a chart, and somebody passed the biscuits.
I was holding the biscuits.

There are a handful of us. We meet in a building in the City that wears its plumbing on the outside, and we decide which of the world's oceans are at war.

I know. I think about it on the Central line, usually somewhere around Bank.

I sit on the Joint War Committee. We are underwriters from Lloyd's and the company market, and we publish a list of Listed Areas: the waters where a ship's ordinary cover stops and a premium for war begins. The men who started this business in Edward Lloyd's coffee house in 1688 did not believe in adjectives, and neither do we.

The building is Richard Rogers's. Lifts, ducts and staircases hang off the outside in stainless steel, so from Lime Street it looks like a refinery that went to Cambridge. I've always thought it the only honest building in the City. Everyone else hides the pipes. Inside, the staff wear navy livery with a flash of red and are called waiters, because 3 centuries ago they poured the coffee. They pour the news now.

In the middle of the Room, under the rostrum, hangs the Lutine Bell. It came off a frigate that went down off the Dutch coast in 1799 with a fortune in gold and silver that Lloyd's had insured, and with 240 people aboard, of whom 1 survived. The market paid for the gold in full and quickly, and that payment made our name. The men were not on the policy. The bell was fished up decades later, and for generations a waiter struck it when news came of an overdue ship: once if she was lost, twice if she'd come home.

During the war, Lord Haw-Haw told Britain the bell was ringing day and night for the convoys. It rang once, for the Bismarck. It is cracked now. The last time it rang for a lost ship was 1979.
Every family has an uncle on the wall. Ours is the slave trade. Our market insured the ships, and in June 2020 Lloyd's apologised for its "shameful" role, which in Lloyd's time is roughly the same afternoon. I mention it because people imagine insurance is neutral. It has never been neutral. It decides which voyages happen.

Here is the whole trick, and it embarrasses people with its simplicity. A ship enters a Listed Area. Her owner tells his insurer. The insurer quotes an additional premium for that one voyage, a percentage of what the hull is worth, good for about a week. The owner pays, or he turns round. Nobody has to sink anything. A number does it.

We don't shout. There is no war room. There is a table, a pot of very bad coffee, and Giles. When a strait has become impossible, Giles reads the reports, takes off his glasses and says "interesting." Everyone at the table knows what interesting means. It means the rate has just tripled. You'd have to have been to the right school to hear the violence in it.

We had competition. On February 28 the Americans and the Israelis struck Iran, and Iran began firing at ships in Hormuz. Before the war, a tanker paid us about 0.25% of her value to pass through. In July the President of the United States published a rate card of his own. Every time Iran fired at a ship, he wrote, America would bomb and destroy "ONE BRIDGE OR POWER PLANT." Capitals in the original.

I admired it enormously. It is a tariff schedule. A man who spent his life in property had priced a strait in infrastructure. The difficulty was that nobody sails on his rate card. Owners do not ring the White House before they leave Fujairah. They ring a broker, the broker rings us, and by summer we were quoting between 3% and 10% of the hull per passage. A $100 million tanker paid $3 million to $10 million for a trip shorter than a bank holiday weekend. Giles said "interesting" 4 times that month.

The President can bomb a bridge. He cannot make a ship sail.
